chunks.text: Northern white-cedar, more commonly sold in nurseries as arborvitae, is a slow-growing conifer of the cypress family native to a cool belt running from southeastern Manitoba through the Great Lakes region into eastern Canada and the northeastern United States, with outlying pockets as far south as the Appalachians. A typical tree stands around 15 metres tall with a trunk under a metre across, though exceptional individuals on favourable sites have reached almost 40 metres; on exposed cliffs and bogs it is often stunted or sprawling instead. Its foliage is made of tiny scale-like leaves pressed flat into fan-shaped sprays, and its small cones, only about a centimetre long, ripen from yellow-green to brown and release roughly eight seeds each. The tree thrives in wet, poorly drained ground such as coniferous swamps where faster, thirstier species cannot compete, and it also colonises bare limestone cliffs where there is almost no competition at all — which is why some of the gnarled, slow-growing individuals rooted in cliff faces around the Great Lakes are now recognised as the oldest trees in eastern North America, with one dated at over 1,140 years and a dead stem showing 1,653 growth rings. Historically its wood went into fence rails, shingles, poles and log construction, and it was the preferred material for the ribs and planking of birchbark and wood-canvas canoes. The Ojibwe call it Nookomis Giizhik, meaning 'Grandmother Cedar', treat it as one of four sacred plants of their medicine wheel, and have long used its vitamin-C-rich foliage and twigs in teas and traditional remedies; one widely repeated account credits the species with curing Jacques Cartier's scurvy-stricken crew in the 1530s, which is also the likely source of the Latin name 'arborvitae', tree of life. Its essential oil, which contains the compound thujone, still finds its way into soaps, disinfectants and insect repellents, though internal use in any quantity is considered unsafe and is not something a home remedy should attempt. Today the species is grown worldwide as a hedging and screening plant, with well over 300 named cultivars in cultivation.

chunks.source: UConn Home & Garden Education Center — Arborvitae factsheet
chunks.text: This University of Connecticut extension factsheet treats arborvitae primarily as a landscape plant rather than a wild forest tree, and its figures reflect cultivated specimens: it gives a mature height range of roughly 40 to 80 feet, taller than the typical wild figure cited by most encyclopedic sources, a reminder that nursery-grown, well-fed trees in the open often outgrow their wild counterparts. It describes the foliage in gardener's terms — flattened sprays of scale-like leaves only about one-sixteenth to one-eighth of an inch long — and notes the small half-inch to three-quarter-inch cones that start green and brown with age. As a practical growing guide aimed at homeowners, the sheet emphasises the plant's long-standing popularity as a privacy screen and formal hedge, its tolerance of a range of soils provided drainage is reasonable, and its vulnerability to winter browsing by deer, which can disfigure or kill young plantings in heavily populated deer country. This kind of source is valuable precisely because it is written for people planting the tree today rather than for taxonomists, giving practical sizing and maintenance expectations that are easy to miss in purely botanical accounts.
